title: The Quiet Cost of a Campus App: Reading Trends, Comparisons and Proportions · 独立口语迁移
instructions: 先完成示范段的跟读诊断，再用不同人物、信息或立场录制自己的完整回答。示范与自由回答分别取证，服务未提供完整听音评阅时保持待评。
reference: In September, a small university in the north of England began a twelve-week trial of a new campus app called CampusFlow. The app was designed to help students find empty study rooms, check library opening hours, and receive alerts about timetable changes. The project team, led by Dr. Helen Marsh, expected the app to reduce the time students spent searching for information. They also hoped it would lower the number of missed classes caused by last-minute room changes. The trial involved 1,200 students across three faculties: Science, Arts, and Business. At the start, 62% of participants said they used paper timetables or noticeboards as their main source of information. Only 18% used the university's existing website, and 20% relied on messages from friends. These baseline figures provided a clear picture of how students accessed information before the app was introduced, and they gave the team a reliable point of comparison for measuring later change.
prompt:
Part 1
Do you often use apps on your phone?
What kind of information do you look for online?
Do you prefer paper or digital timetables? Why?
How do you remind yourself about appointments?

Part 2
Describe a time when a new tool or app was introduced at your school or workplace. You should say: what the tool was; who used it; what changed after it was introduced; and explain whether you think it was a success.

Part 3
Why do some people prefer email to apps for reminders?
What problems can happen when a new technology is introduced?
Should universities collect more data about student attendance? Why?
How can we compare the real effects of a new tool with its expected effects?
